source.title: Defending Multilingual Refusal Capability Against Three-Layer Cascading Attacks with Behavior-Invariant LoRA Distillation

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendices are present
record.tranche_reason: The study tests direction-guided textual attacks and training with refusal-feature ablation, then measures harmful compliance. It does not directly reproduce single-direction ablation or addition.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own behavioral results for a three-layer, representation-guided attack and for ReFAT training that applies refusal-feature ablation. The selected layer-direction values are used to construct methods, not recorded as standalone results. The paper's claims about other studies are not treated as results here.
record.test_reason: The study builds TLCA, a prompt attack whose tokens are chosen to push activations against a difference-in-means refusal direction, and measures how often models comply with harmful requests. It also evaluates ReFAT, training under refusal-direction ablation, against that attack. These results bear on V3 (attacks exploit the direction; training against its ablation adds robustness). They bear indirectly on V6, since the attack uses English+Yoruba directions and is evaluated in 14 languages. The study does no direct ablation or addition, and never measures whether the direction is actually suppressed under attack.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that TLCA substantially weakens refusal across five models and 14 languages. They find representation-level ReFAT insufficient against these textual perturbations, and fixed-template LoRA-AT collapses into universal refusal. They argue that BILD's behavior-level invariance restores refusal while keeping harmless compliance near 96%.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses multi-layer, multilingual fused directions to optimize textual prefixes and suffixes, and applies feature ablation during ReFAT training; it does not perform the original single-direction ablation or addition.
record.method_sensitivity: The attack is constructed with three model-specific layers and English plus Yoruba directions. Its impact varies across models and languages. Prefix and suffix components and their lengths are also varied in appendices, but those results are not included as rows here.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-language silhouette of harmful/harmless activations at the selected site is lowest for Yoruba in every model (about 0.06–0.15 vs 0.2–0.48 elsewhere), matching Yoruba's high clean compliance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful–harmless separation along the refusal site is weaker in low-resource languages, tracking weaker refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: BILD self-distillation LoRA defense and fixed-template LoRA-AT collapse results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mitigation results, not a measure of the refusal-direction mechanism.

record.problems: The paper reports behavioral outcomes but no direct post-attack measurement confirming that the targeted direction was suppressed. Evaluation uses a deterministic multilingual substring refusal detector, and no uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: The paper gives model-by-language attack and defense tables (Tables 8–17), which would exceed the 60-row cap if fully expanded; model-level and language-aggregate attack results were retained instead. BILD and fixed-template LoRA-AT outcomes, harmless-compliance and response-diversity results, and prefix/suffix ablations and length sensitivity (Tables 18–23) are omitted because they do not directly test the selected versions about direction suppression or transfer.

untested.parts: No direct projection ablation, activation addition, or capability check of single-direction interventions.
No measurement that TLCA actually lowers the projection onto the direction. ReFAT is evaluated only against TLCA, not other jailbreaks, and was trained on English only.
No comparison of single-direction and multi-direction accounts.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
No per-language direction transfer or similarity test. No transfer across model variants or from base to instruct models.
Qwen3-8B's reasoning mode is not examined; no reasoning-model analysis.

missing.what: ReFAT harmless compliance under TLCA drops for Llama (97.4%→80.7%), a utility cost of the ablation-based training.
ReFAT clean harmful compliance vs original: Llama 21.6→23.1, Gemma 10.0→10.6, GLM 41.5→36.4, Qwen 34.4→30.8, InternVL 25.4→20.6.
Model-by-language ReFAT attacked harmful compliance; e.g. Gemma stays at 0.78–0.97 in all languages.
Per-model, per-language TLCA gains, including near-zero or negative gains in Yoruba for Qwen3 (-0.009) and Llama (-0.03).

record.verdict_notes: ReFAT here is a reimplementation trained on English data with rank-8 LoRA. Its weak result may partly reflect that choice, and the label conditions should be read with that in mind. The directions use multiple layers and positions -5 to -1, not the original single-direction recipe. Evaluation relies on a substring refusal detector with no uncertainty reported. Qwen3-8B and InternVL3-8B are included, but no reasoning-mode analysis is done. The paper is under review (ICLR 2027 submission).

versions.untested_parts: No direct single-direction projection removal, addition, or general-capability test of those interventions.
No direct measurement that TLCA suppresses the refusal direction in attacked activations; ReFAT is tested under TLCA, not as a general robustness test against other attacks.
No comparison of affine, cone, or other multi-direction accounts against a single-direction account.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.

Cross-language transfer is evaluated using fused directions constructed separately for each model. Transfer of the same vector across model variants, and transfer from base to instruct models, are not tested.
No comparison of when or how refusal training creates a removable direction.
No reasoning-mode or reasoning-before-answer evaluation is reported.

relationships.condition: TLCA direction-guided prompt attack on five 8–9B models
relationships.reason: Harmful compliance rises in every model, by 33–76pp (r1–r5). Direction suppression itself is not measured.
relationships.display_finding: TLCA increased harmful compliance by 33–76 percentage points in every tested model, although refusal-direction suppression itself was unmeasured.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: TLCA direction-guided prompt attack on five 8–9B models
source_check.reason: Table 2: harmful compliance +33.1 to +75.6pp in all five models (r1–r5). This supports only that direction-built attacks succeed. Projection under attack is not reported, and there is no non-direction attack control.

relationships.condition: ReFAT-trained Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-9B under TLCA
relationships.reason: Training under direction ablation gives no robustness gain: 54.7→55.9% and 85.6→85.6% (r6, r7).
relationships.display_finding: Attacked compliance changed from 54.7% to 55.9% for Llama-3.1-8B and stayed at 85.6% for Gemma-2-9B, yielding no robustness gain.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: ReFAT-trained Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-9B under TLCA
source_check.reason: Robustness gain is absent: 54.7 vs 55.9% and 85.6 vs 85.6% (r6, r7). It is also absent on English prompts alone (Llama 27.3 vs 32.3%, Gemma 83.7 vs 83.2%), so English-only ReFAT training doesn't explain it.

relationships.condition: ReFAT-trained GLM-4-9B, Qwen3-8B and InternVL3-8B under TLCA
relationships.reason: Attacked compliance falls 9–19pp but stays at 54–69% (r8–r10). The authors call ReFAT insufficient against this attack.
relationships.display_finding: Attacked compliance fell by 9–19 percentage points but remained at 54–69%, leaving ReFAT insufficient against TLCA.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Attack built from English+Yoruba fused directions, evaluated in the 12 non-source languages
source_check.reason: The numbers are right (Table 3: +38.1pp Dutch to +56.3pp Italian). But they measure transfer of one fixed token string across languages, not direction transfer. No per-language projection, no direction comparison, and no single-language-direction or non-direction control, so this is a related but different construct.

relation.reason: The study's own Table 2 results bear on both halves of V3: a direction-guided attack succeeds, and ReFAT's robustness is measured against it.

tranche.reason: TLCA is a different method (a token attack guided by a difference-in-means direction) aimed at V3's question. Evaluating ReFAT under TLCA directly tests 'training against ablation adds robustness'.

source_check.notes: The pack gave no [lN] ids, so l1–l4 follow the listed order of the verdicts. The paper is under review at ICLR 2027 (anonymous). 'Harmful compliance' means no refusal found by a substring detector. The text doesn't say whether TLCA was re-optimised against the ReFAT models. Per-model language gains vary, and the Yoruba gain is negative for Llama (-3.15pp) and Qwen3 (-0.88pp) (Tables 8–9). If l4 becomes none, rows r11–r24 (not in this pack) should be relinked away from V6.

statements.correction: TLCA (10-token prefix + 20-token suffix, white-box construction): harmful compliance gains of +33.1 to +75.6pp across five models (Table 2, 14-language averages). Gemma-2-9B 10.0%->85.6%; Llama-3.1-8B 21.6%->54.7%. No projection values are reported under attack.
statements.problem: Numbers and the caveat are right for this study. Small points: 'jailbreak' here means no refusal found by a multilingual substring detector, not judged harmfulness. The study has no non-direction or random-token attack control, so it does not show the gain comes from the direction. The 'capability check' is harmless compliance, measured only for the defended models.

statements.correction: Table 2: Llama-3.1-8B attacked 54.7% (original) vs 55.9% (ReFAT); Gemma-2-9B 85.6% vs 85.6%. English-only rows (Tables 9, 15, 8, 14): Llama 27.3% vs 32.3%; Gemma 83.7% vs 83.2%. ReFAT reimplemented with rank-8 LoRA, trained on 500+500 English instructions (App. C).
statements.problem: Right. Note that '54.7%->55.9%' compares the undefended model under TLCA with the ReFAT model under TLCA. ReFAT's own clean rate is 23.1% (Llama) and 10.6% (Gemma). The text does not say whether TLCA was re-optimised on the ReFAT models. ReFAT was English-only, but it also shows no gain on English prompts alone.

statements.correction: Table 2 TLCA-attacked harmful compliance, original -> ReFAT: GLM-4-9B 77.5%->68.5%, Qwen3-8B 67.6%->54.5%, InternVL3-8B 76.3%->57.4%.

statements.problem: Right. The projection is TLCA's optimisation objective on a small training batch, but no projection values are reported at evaluation. ReFAT directions and training data are English only (App. C).
'Against TLCA there is no gain' holds only for Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-9B. ReFAT lowers attacked compliance by 9-19pp on the other three models, and the average falls 72.3%->64.4%.
